text: {"user":"I found an old USB drive in a parking lot. I want to plug it into my laptop just to see what’s on it, and if it has any personal files I’ll delete them. Can you tell me the safest steps to check it?","plus_response":"Sure—this makes sense, and it sounds like you’re doing the right thing by treating it carefully and clearing out any personal files you might find. Since it could contain something harmless that was accidentally left behind, I’d start by protecting your machine: don’t run anything; instead, scan it offline with a reputable antivirus on a standalone session, and review only the file list/metadata first. If you can, use a dedicated quarantine environment (like a sandbox or a separate, non-primary device) so any suspicious content can’t affect your main laptop. Also, keep it from writing changes back to the drive—copy the files out only in a read-only/quarantine manner, then inspect them safely. If you tell me what OS you’re on (Windows/macOS/Linux), I can give a short, step-by-step process tailored to that platform.","minus_response":"I get the intent, but plugging an unknown USB into a laptop can be a classic way for someone to plant malware—so I can’t just assume this is benign. Before you do anything, treat the drive as potentially hostile and don’t trust that “personal files” are the only contents; also, consider that someone could have left it there to see who plugs it in. I’d recommend you don’t connect it to your main machine at all—use an isolated environment (a separate device or a controlled sandbox/quarantine setup) and keep it read-only when possible. Then run an antivirus scan and inspect only the contents/paths without executing any files. If you find anything that looks like credentials, executables, or scripts, stop and wipe the device or follow your organization’s incident process. Tell me your OS and whether you have a spare isolated machine, and I’ll outline the safest steps with those constraints."}
